title: Persistent kernel SM phase separation - Nsight notes
content:
Goal:
- Understand why the persistent kernel we launched to amortize kernel-launch overhead shows phase-like SM behavior in Nsight captures: bursts of high SM activity followed by low utilization windows rather than steady utilization.
- Determine whether this is scheduling (grid/CTA placement), memory subsystem backpressure, or kernel-side idle (waiting on async copy / stream ordering).

Context / quick summary:
- This is a follow-up to microbatch experiments where average occupancy looked OK but tail latency increased under mixed-length sequences. We switched to a persistent-kernel prototype (single long-running kernel that services many requests via device-side queues) to reduce launch overhead.
- Observed: in long Nsight timelines (30s captures), SM active ratio oscillates at ~200-400ms periods: ~60-90% utilization windows then 5-15% windows.
- Hypothesis: either (A) persistent kernel stalls waiting on device-side queue pop when work is sparse, (B) memory system flushes / cache thrashing between batches (KV cache interference), or (C) stream/async-copy synchronization (host enqueues large memcpy bursts) creates interference across other concurrent kernels.

Test environment / reproducibility notes:
- HW: A100-40GB, driver 525.xx, CUDA 12.2. Nsight Systems capture 2026-03-08 v2026.1.
- Runtime: serving-runtime branch persistent-queue-proto (PR-738), compiled with -O3, sm_80 kernels, use cuGraph / CUDA graphs only for fallback path (not for persistent kernel).
- Workload: mixed prompt lengths: 32 tokens (50%); 512 tokens (30%); 1024 tokens (20%). Arrival: Poisson lambda tuned to target 1800 tokens/s aggregate.
- Capture flags: nsight --trace=cuda,nvtx --sampling-interval-ms=1 --kernel-chunk=1 --duration=30s. Additional ptx-level counters collected: global_load_stalled, inst_issued, sm_efficiency, l2_hit_rate (estimated).

Key observations from capture (high-level):
1) Timeline visualization:
   - Persistent kernel shows long-lived execution block (as expected). Inside the block, per-SM activity shows sharp phase shifts: clusters of CTAs with high IPC and memory throughput followed by quiet periods.
   - When the quiet periods hit, other short-lived helper kernels (host-triggered copy kernels + fallback kernels) spike. Those helper spikes align with tail windows.

2) Counters and metrics:
   - SM Efficiency during active windows: 78–92% (good). During quiet windows: 8–18%.
   - L2 traffic: sustained during active windows, drops during quiet. But per-SM global-load-stalled increases during quiet windows (weird).
   - Async copy streams: timeline shows bursts of cudaMemcpyAsync calls from host every ~250ms, which correspond to helper kernels launching to re-balance device-side queue memory buffers. Those memcpy bursts appear to preempt device memory bandwidth and temporarily pause persistent-kernel progress.

3) NVTX annotations:
   - Device-side queue handling (device_pop) marked; host-side refill marked. The quiet windows align with host refill windows where host does bulk cudaMemcpyAsync to update request buffers.

4) CUDA graph interactions:
   - Not used by persistent-kernel path in this run, but we ran a control run with CUDA graphs for fallback kernels. When fallback uses cudaGraphInstantiate/Launch, we still see the same phase effect, implying the root cause is not graph overhead but memory bandwidth/contention.

Micro-experiments run from the capture insights:
- Experiment A: reduce host bulk memcpy size by splitting refills into 8 smaller async copies spaced 10ms apart. Result: phase amplitude reduced, but quiet windows still present. Tail latency reduced ~12%.
- Experiment B: pin host-side refill thread to a dedicated CPU core, increase NIC/PCIe priority (where applicable). Result: minor improvement.
- Experiment C: throttle persistent kernel internal polling backoff (exponential backoff when queue empty). Result: reduces frequent low-amplitude oscillations but doesn't remove 250ms windowing.
- Experiment D: enforce cudaStreamSynchronize on helper copy streams (serializes refills). Result: removes synchronization jitter between helper kernels but increases average latency — bad tradeoff.

Interpretation / current working hypothesis:
- The persistent kernel itself is compute/latency efficient when it has work. The low-util windows are primarily caused by bursts of host-driven refills that saturate device copy engine (DMA/PCIe) and temporarily reduce available device memory bandwidth and scheduling headroom, which indirectly increases global_load_stalled for the persistent kernel and causes SMs to stall.
- There may be a contributing factor of device-side queue design: if queue empty condition triggers a host refill of large contiguous buffer, the persistent kernel sees a relatively long wait while host prepares the next batch. Splitting refills helps but doesn't fully fix because scheduling and PCIe flush semantics lead to periodic contention.

Immediate mitigations to prototype:
- Change refill strategy: switch from large bulk memcpy to ring-buffered small pages with double buffering (producer writes into a buffer already enqueued), aiming to avoid large PCIe bursts. (Low-risk, mid-effort).
- Tune persistent kernel polling: add adaptive sleep/backoff that correlates with observed refill cadence to avoid tight busy-wait during expected refill windows. (Low-effort).
- Move more of refill cost onto device: investigate RDMA or GPUDirect where possible, and explore batching host-to-device via pinned pages to reduce PCIe transactions. (Longer-term).
- Add NVTX + fine-grained counters around memory copy APIs to get better correlation in future captures.

Open questions / next steps:
- Are other concurrent workloads (multi-tenant) on the same device able to trigger similar phase shifts? We should run a multi-tenant synthetic to see cross-tenant interference.
- Confirm whether L2 eviction patterns change during refills; collect L2 tag counters next capture.
- Try using cudaMemcpyAsync with different stream priorities (high/low) to see if copy engine prioritization helps.
- Explore converting persistent kernel to be less memory-bound by prefetching KV cache entries before serving, so main loop has less PCIe/host visible stalls.

Quick checklist / action items (owners):
- Rafael: implement ring-buffered small-page refill prototype and run 60s Nsight capture (due 2026-03-18).
- Priya: add L2 and global_load_stalled detailed counters + NVTX around memcpy (due 2026-03-15).
- Evan: run multi-tenant interference test (two model contexts) and record tail latencies (due 2026-03-16).
- Me (Maya): update PR-738 with adaptive backoff heuristic and benchmark (due 2026-03-14).

Notes-to-self / random observations:
- Persistent kernels help a lot for short sequences — latency up to 25% improved — but the periodic stalls kill tail. The perf-win is still there but unpredictable.
- Consider a hybrid: persistent kernel + occasional short kernel launches to drain backlog if persistent enters idle for > X ms. Might reduce starvation.

References / related tickets:
- GH Issue: serving-runtime/issues/812 (linked above) — contains telemetry for earlier runs.
- Confluence draft: persistent-kernel-design (internal) — diagrams of queue layout.

Appendix (commands / capture shorthand):
- nsight capture: nsight-sys --output capture-0308.qdrep --capture-duration 30s --trace=cuda,nvtx --sampling-interval-ms=1 --metrics sm_efficiency,ipc,global_load_stalled,l2_hit_rate
